transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. To start, can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
I don’t feel like myself anymore. I barely talk to people—I just kind of go flat and quiet. And getting started on my cleaning route feels like pushing a loaded cart uphill.
How long have you been feeling this way—flat, quiet, and low in energy?
About a year and five months now. It started building after I had to leave my old apartment and neighborhood.
Have you ever had a period, lasting several days or more, where you felt unusually energetic, elated, or needed much less sleep than usual—very different from your low mood now?
No, I can’t say I’ve had a stretch like that. I haven’t noticed being unusually energetic or needing a lot less sleep.
Over this past year and five months, have there been any stretches of two months or longer where you felt essentially back to your normal self, without the low mood or fatigue?

No, not really. Since the move, the sadness and low energy have mostly stayed in the background. I feel guilty and don’t have much interest in things, even when the voices or the camera worries are what I’m focused on that day.
Do you experience the voices or the feeling that you're being watched by cameras even during times when your mood feels less low, or do they only happen when you're feeling depressed?

There were a few weeks when my mood was a little better—I was eating and getting through work better—but I still heard my name in the stairwell. And I still believed the hallway cameras were being used to track me.
During that stretch when your mood felt a bit better, about how many weeks did it last while you were still hearing your name and believing the cameras were tracking you?
It was several weeks, I’d say. I was doing a little better with meals and work, but I still heard my name in the stairwell and was convinced the hallway cameras were tracking me.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient has a prolonged depressive syndrome (17 months) with anhedonia, guilt, and low energy following a psychosocial stressor (forced relocation), meeting criteria for a depressive episode. Concurrently, she has persistent psychotic symptoms—auditory hallucinations (hearing her name called) and persecutory delusions (belief that hallway cameras are tracking her). Critically, during a period of several weeks when her depressive symptoms partially remitted (improved appetite and functioning), the hallucinations and delusions persisted, demonstrating that psychotic symptoms occur independently of the mood disturbance for a period ≥2 weeks. No manic or hypomanic episode was ever reported, ruling out the bipolar subtype. The co-occurrence of mood and psychotic symptoms most of the time, combined with psychotic symptoms extending beyond the mood episode, is most consistent with Schizoaffective Disorder, depressive type (F25.1), rather than Major Depressive Disorder with psychotic features (which would require psychotic symptoms only during mood episodes) or Schizophrenia (which would require psychotic symptoms to dominate independent of significant mood symptoms).
